fields.h1: What Is Surrender to God, and How Do I Actually Do It?
fields.meta_title: What Is Surrender to God, and How Do I Actually Do It?
fields.description: Christians talk about surrendering to God — but what does it mean, and why does it lead to freedom rather than loss? Here is what surrender is and how to do it.
fields.body_html:
“Surrender to God” is one of those phrases Christians use constantly and rarely define. It can sound like defeat — giving up, losing control, handing over your dreams. And so we hold back, suspecting that surrender means becoming less. Yet the people who have surrendered most deeply to God are almost always the freest, most joyful people you will meet. How can that be? Because surrender to God is not the loss of your life but the finding of it — and it is the doorway to a freedom you cannot reach any other way. Everything hinges, in the end, on the kind of God you are surrendering to; and once you see that he is a Father who gave his own Son for you, the whole question changes.

Here is what surrender actually is, why it leads to freedom rather than loss, and how to do it in practice.

What surrender means

To surrender to God is to hand him the whole of your life — your will, your plans, your fears, your rights — and to accept his will in their place. Paul frames it as an offering: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). Not part of yourself, kept back for emergencies; the whole self, laid on the altar. Surrender is the moment you stop being the lord of your own life and let God be Lord in fact as well as in name.

Jesus made this the very condition of following him: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). To deny yourself is not self-hatred; it is dethroning the self that insists on running everything, so that Christ can reign. Andrew Murray gave his classic little book on this one word its bold title — Absolute Surrender — because he was convinced that a partial surrender is the reason so many Christians live weak, joyless lives. God can only fully bless what is fully given to him.

What surrender is not

Because the word is easily misread, it helps to clear away some false ideas. Surrender is not passivity — a limp giving-up that stops caring or striving. The surrendered person is often the most active and courageous of all, precisely because they are no longer paralyzed by self-protection. It is not the loss of your personality or your dreams; God more often purifies and enlarges what we hand him than erases it. It is not a single dramatic experience that settles the matter forever — it is a posture returned to daily. And it is not earning God’s love; you do not surrender to make God accept you, but because he already has, at the cost of his Son. Surrender is not a fearful capitulation to a tyrant. It is the glad yielding of a child to a Father who is wiser and kinder than we are, and who has never once misused a life entrusted to him.

Why we resist it

If surrender is so good, why do we fight it? Because we quietly believe the lie that God is a hard master who will strip us of everything we love if we let him. We cling to control because we do not fully trust the One we are asked to trust. But surrender is only as safe as the God you surrender to — and this God is a Father who gave his own Son for you. To hand your life to a God like that is not reckless; it is the most reasonable thing you could do. As Paul reasoned, “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” The safest place in the entire universe, it turns out, is the center of the will of a God who has loved you all the way to a cross.

Why surrender leads to freedom, not loss

Here is the paradox at the heart of the Christian life: “whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it” (Mark 8:35). The self we grip so tightly, we lose — it shrinks, sours, and enslaves us to a hundred fears about protecting it. The self we surrender to Christ, we receive back, alive and free. Paul described the exchange from the inside: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). What looks from the outside like the end of you is actually the beginning of a far larger life — Christ’s own life, lived through you.

Hannah Whitall Smith called her famous book on this The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life, because she had found that the path of full surrender is also the path of deep rest. When you have handed everything to God, there is nothing left to anxiously guard. The surrendered heart can say, whatever comes, “this too is in my Father’s hands.” That is not the language of loss; it is the language of freedom.

Surrender and the deeper life

Surrender is also the gateway to what Murray, in The Master’s Indwelling, called the deeper Christian life — the life no longer of a believer struggling in their own strength, but of Christ living his life through a yielded vessel. You cannot be filled while you are still full of yourself; you cannot be led while you insist on choosing the way. The Spirit fills and leads what is surrendered to him. This is why surrender is not a one-time crisis to get past but a settled posture to maintain — a daily, and sometimes hourly, handing back of the control we keep taking up again. There is often a decisive first surrender — a definite moment when a Christian, perhaps years after conversion, finally gives God everything — and that moment can genuinely transform a life. But it is kept and deepened only by countless small surrenders afterward, in the ordinary decisions and disappointments of each day, where we discover again how tightly we grip and choose again to let go. Do not be discouraged that you must keep surrendering the same things; that is not failure but the very texture of a life increasingly given to God.

How to actually surrender

Surrender is a decision before it is a feeling, and you can make it today. A few steps:

  • Make a definite act of surrender. In prayer, deliberately give God everything — your future, your relationships, your ambitions, your fears, your rights — naming the things you have been holding back. “Submit yourselves therefore to God” (James 4:7). This decisive yes matters, even before any feeling changes.
  • Surrender the specific thing. General surrender is easy; the real test is the particular fear, plan, or person you most want to control. Hand God the exact thing your grip is closed around.
  • Trust his character. “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5). Surrender rests on the goodness of the One you surrender to; feed your trust on who he is.
  • Renew it daily. You will take the control back; when you notice, simply give it again. Surrender is a habit of the heart, learned over a lifetime.
  • Count the trade honestly. Like Paul, “I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). You are not throwing your life away; you are exchanging fool’s gold for the real thing.

God does not ask for your surrender because he wants to take from you, but because he wants to give you himself — and he cannot fill hands that are clenched shut. Open them. What you release into his keeping was never as safe in yours, and what he gives in return is a life, and a freedom, and a peace that clutching could never buy.

If full surrender still feels frightening, begin where you are. You do not have to feel ready; you have to be willing — and if you are not even willing, you can ask God to make you so. Tell him honestly what you are afraid to give up, and ask him for the grace to open your hand. He is patient with a heart that is genuinely turning toward him, and he never despises the smallest step in his direction. Andrew Murray watched countless struggling Christians come into rest and power the moment they stopped bargaining with God and simply gave him everything. The same is on offer to you. The surrendered life is not the narrow, grey thing we fear; it is the widest, freest, most joyful life a human being can live — because it is life with the hand of God, no longer resisted, free at last to bless.
